output.brief: The evidence points mainly to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Yield fell only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's went from 45.2% to 31.9%, and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield held at about 36%. The no-award group held at about 37–38%. That pattern rules out a general softening in demand. The applicant pool was larger and as strong as before, so it was not the cause. Early-action yield also fell, from 45.2% to 37.8%. Those students got decisions on time under the old system, so the slow portal is not the main driver. Slower regular-decision turnaround is real, but it does not explain the yield drop. I'm fairly confident in this (about 80%). I could not separate the schedule's effect from other factors by round within tier. The missing-document problem is unverified. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly-reported decision-turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the document problem is checked.
